Render a keyframe animation

Source: R/animate.R
vl_render_animation.Rd

Interpolate between a set of compiled keyframe scenes and encode the in-between frames to an animated image, in one parallel, streaming pass in the Rust backend. This is the low-level engine a grammar layer (e.g. vellumplot's animate()) drives: the caller supplies the K keyframe scenes and a per-frame schedule — for each output frame, which adjacent keyframe pair to interpolate and the eased fraction between them — and this renders and encodes every frame.

Usage

vl_render_animation(
  keyframes,
  seg,
  frac,
  path,
  format = c("gif", "apng", "svg", "frames"),
  fps = 25,
  gif_speed = 10,
  gif_dither = TRUE,
  frac_col = NULL,
  frac_size = NULL,
  frac_alpha = NULL,
  text_variants = NULL,
  text_frame = NULL
)

Arguments

keyframes

A list of at least two scenes (each a vl_scene() or anything with an as_vellum_scene() method), all the same pixel size.

seg

Integer vector, one entry per output frame: the 1-based index of the frame's left keyframe (it is interpolated with keyframe seg + 1).

frac

Numeric vector, one per output frame: the eased interpolation fraction in [0, 1] (0 = the left keyframe, 1 = the right one). Same length as seg. This is the schedule for positional geometry, and for every discrete attribute that snaps at the halfway point.

path

Output path: an image file for "gif"/"apng"/"svg", or a directory (created if needed) for "frames".

format

"gif" (looping animated GIF), "apng" (animated PNG), "svg" (a single animated SVG), or "frames" (one frameNNNNN.png per frame into path).

fps

Frames per second (sets each frame's on-screen duration). Need not be whole: 12.5 or 0.5 (a two-second slideshow frame) are kept exactly. A GIF stores delays in whole centiseconds, so its rate is the nearest 100 / n fps, and above 50 fps browsers play it slower, not faster (a warning says so).

gif_speed

GIF only: the NeuQuant palette sample factor, 1 (best quality, slowest) to 30 (fastest). The default 10 samples a tenth of the pixels to build each frame's palette: with dithering on, the frames are visually indistinguishable from 1 on a plot (a mean error under 0.2 of 255 per channel on a dense scatter), at about a quarter of the encode time. Use 1 for the last bit of palette fidelity. Ignored for "apng"/"svg"/"frames".

gif_dither

GIF only: apply Floyd–Steinberg dithering (default TRUE), which greatly reduces the banding a 256-colour palette leaves on gradients and antialiased edges. A frame that already fits in 256 colours is kept exact.

frac_col, frac_size, frac_alpha

Optional per-aesthetic schedules, each a numeric vector the same length as frac, for the colour, size and opacity classes respectively. NULL (the default) uses frac, so one easing curve shapes the whole scene. Supplying a differently-eased vector lets each aesthetic travel on its own curve — position arriving on cubic-in-out while colour crossfades linear, say. See Per-aesthetic easing below.

text_variants, text_frame

Optional per-frame text, for a label that changes on every frame rather than only at keyframes (a title showing the current time, say). text_variants is a list of scenes (anything with an as_vellum_scene() method), each holding one or more keyed text grobs (text_grob(key = )); text_frame gives, per output frame, the 1-based index of the variant that frame uses, or 0 (or NA) for none. In a frame that uses a variant, every keyed text node of the tweened frame whose key matches one of the variant's text grobs takes that grob's string and glyph layout (shaping, extent, font and size), while its position, rotation, justification and colour stay as the tween put them. So shape each distinct string once, with the same font and wrapping width as the node it replaces. NULL (the default) for neither.

Value

path, invisibly.

Details

The frames are tweened at the scene level: matching primitives interpolate their geometry, their colours (perceptually, in Oklab), and their bounded graphical parameters; discrete attributes snap. Nothing retrains between frames — the keyframes are fixed at author time — so this is non-reactive keyframe animation, not a live/reactive runtime.

GIF is limited to 256 colours per frame, so on a plot (smooth panels, antialiased marks) it is inherently lossy — gif_speed/gif_dither make it as clean as that palette allows. For a lossless result use format = "apng".

Each GIF frame is quantised to its own palette and dithered on the worker threads that rasterise it, so a GIF encodes in parallel like the other formats; it is still several times slower than APNG (a 1200 x 800, 150-frame scatter: about 3 s against 2 s for APNG at the default gif_speed, 13 s at gif_speed = 1).

Choosing a format

"svg" emits every frame as vector markup, shown in turn by a CSS step animation. It is resolution-independent, which no raster format is — the same file is crisp in a slide, on a retina screen and in print.

Its size depends on scene complexity in a way the raster formats' does not, because every frame is emitted in full. Measured on a 30-frame scatter animation, gzipped (which is how a browser will fetch it):

marksanimated SVG (gzipped)GIF
2020 KB61 KB
20080 KB296 KB
2000720 KB124 KB

So it wins clearly on line art — an explanatory animation of a few moving marks, which is the common case — and loses on a dense scatter, where a raster format is the right answer. Serve it gzipped (.svgz, or any web server with compression on); uncompressed it is several times larger again.

It also honours prefers-reduced-motion: a reader who has asked their system not to animate gets one still frame. That is the last frame when the schedule ends exactly on the final keyframe (a reveal, a time series, a sequence that does not loop: the complete picture), and the first frame otherwise (a loop).

Its CSS class and animation names carry the document's id prefix, so several animated SVGs inlined into one HTML page play independently.

Matching marks by identity

Marks are matched across keyframes by their data keys (a grob's keys, the same keys interactivity uses), not by where they sit in the node list. An element keyed "k" in one keyframe tweens into the element keyed "k" in the next wherever that is drawn: in another node, at another index, in another colour group's batch (a point that changes group slides and recolours). So the order of rows, and which groups a state happens to contain, do not matter. Keys are matched across the whole scene, so a caller keeps them unique per layer (vellumplot prefixes the layer) and stable across states.

What has no partner enters or leaves:

  • keyed points, circles, rectangles (bars, tiles), hexagons, sectors and segments, and keyed lines, polygons, paths, rounded rectangles and text labels fade in or out on the alpha schedule;

  • unkeyed nodes (axes, gridlines, legends, unkeyed marks) pair in order with the nodes of the same viewport, kind and role in the other keyframe. When that class has a different number of nodes in the two keyframes it cannot be matched, and its nodes switch whole at the midpoint (frac >= 0.5).

A matched line, polygon or path whose vertex count changes morphs: both outlines are put on one common set of vertices by arc length (every vertex of either, at its fraction of the way along its own outline), and a ring is first turned to run the same way round and start near the other's start. Each keeps all of its own vertices, so the morph starts and ends on the keyframes exactly. A pair in mixed or different units, with a stroke-width profile, a broken (non-finite) line, or paths with different numbers of sub-paths, switches whole at the midpoint instead, as does a matched pair of different kinds; a text label takes its string and layout from the nearer keyframe while its position tweens.

Marks that overlap are drawn in the left keyframe's order up to the midpoint and in the right keyframe's from there on, so a mark that moves in front of another swaps over halfway through the move, along with the other discrete switches, rather than popping at the next keyframe.

Two keyframes that do not share a viewport tree cannot be matched at all: the frames show the left keyframe up to the midpoint and the right one from there on (a cut, but every keyframe is shown). vl_tween_pairing() reports all of this before rendering. Easing curves that overshoot (back, elastic) may carry positions past their targets, but sizes, radii and line widths stay at or above zero and opacity within [0, 1].

Per-aesthetic easing

frac and its three companions carry one eased fraction per property class, so a single frame can interpolate different properties at different points along their transitions. Every drawn property belongs to exactly one class:

scheduledrives
fracx/y and all coordinate geometry, widths and heights, angles, path vertices, text rotation, dash phase — and every discrete attribute's halfway snap (lty, lineend, labels, a variant mismatch)
frac_colfill, col, the stroke paint, and per-element colour vectors (hexagon and sector fills)
frac_sizelwd, marker size, circle and corner radius, hexagon extent, linemitre
frac_alphaalpha, including the enter/exit fade — a keyed element appearing or leaving fades on this curve

Two consequences worth knowing. Easing alpha retimes entrances and exits, not just explicit opacity changes. And because a discrete attribute flips when its fraction crosses 0.5, and an eased curve reaches 0.5 at a different frame than a linear one, frac decides which frame those snaps land on.

Passing all four identical (the default) reproduces single-curve easing exactly — the output is byte-identical to omitting them.

See also

render(), as_vellum_scene()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
grow <- lapply(c(0.1, 0.3, 0.2), function(r) {
  vl_scene(3, 2) |> draw(circle_grob(r = r, gp = vl_gpar(fill = "tomato")))
})
# 15 frames per move (fraction 0 up to, not including, 1 -- the next move
# starts on that keyframe), then 10 frames held on the last keyframe.
seg <- c(rep(1:2, each = 15), rep(2, 10))
frac <- c(rep((0:14) / 15, 2), rep(1, 10))
vl_render_animation(grow, seg, frac, tempfile(fileext = ".gif"))
} # }
